conversation.content: You are an impartial summarization judge.

Evaluate two candidate summaries against the Human Reference Summary using this rubric: - Content Coverage (0–4): captures main contributions, methodology, key findings - Accuracy (0–3): technically correct, no factual errors - Clarity & Structure (0–2): organized, readable, logical flow - Conciseness (0–1): covers essentials without fluff Human Reference Summary: ${file:documents/arxiv-2508-08314v1/abstract.md} Candidate A: **Summary** | Aspect | Description | |--------|-------------| | **Research question** | Can generative large language models (LLMs) automatically produce high‑quality, course‑specific multiple‑choice assessments that are on par with human‑crafted exam items? | | **Main contribution** | *A scalable, iterative “Self‑Refine”–style pipeline* to generate, evaluate, and select exam questions tailored to any college course, followed by the **largest‑ever field study** (≈1,200 students, 91 courses) that psychometrically compares AI‑generated items with human‑crafted questions from a standardised test. | | **Generation pipeline** | 1. **Prompt‑matching**: include course description, syllabus, previous exams, and five exemplar AP‑statistics items.
2. **Generate → Judge → Refine loop** (≈~20 “good” MCQs):
  • LLM (OpenAI o3‑mini) writes one MCQ in JSON.
  • An AI judge scores the question (“Good” / “Bad”) based on relevance, length, conceptual depth, and absence of logistical info.
  • The judged Q&A pair is added to the next prompt as a further example (up to 5 good / 5 bad).
3. **Final vetting**: another judge checks correct answer, sanity, and difficulty; the top‑10 hardest pass the exam.
4. **Fallback** if >10 questions fail, generate 20 additional items and re‑rank. | | **Benchmark setup** | Same student cohort took **AI‑generated** exams (71 courses) or **AP‑Statistics‑practice‑exam** questions (20 courses).
Pre‑test of quantitative reasoning was used to anchor a common ability scale across groups. | | **Analytical method** | Hierarchical Bayesian 2‑ logistic Item Response Theory (IRT):
• Item difficulty (β), discrimination (α).
• Student ability θ pooled via reference pre‑test.
• Posterior predictive checks show good calibration; convergence (R̂ < 1.05). | | **Key psychometric findings** | • **Difficulty**: AI items easier on average (β̄​AI = –0.45 vs. β̄​STD = 0.35, Δβ = –0.79, 95 % CI [–0.94, –0.65]).
• **Discrimination**: AI items marginally higher (ᾱ​AI = 1.30 vs. ᾱ​STD = 1.20, Δα = 0.09, 95 % CI [–0.09, 0.25], P≈0.85).
• **Test information**: AI exams peak at I(θ) = 3.85 (R = 0.79) at θ ≈ –0.51; standardised item sets peak at I(θ) = 2.61 (R = 0.72) at θ ≈ 0.32.
• In short, AI‑generated 10‑question exams provide comparable or superior discrimination, especially for below‑average students, while still covering the full ability spectrum. | | **Limitations noted** | • Bench‑mark restricted to statistics courses (AP questions).
• Multiple‑choice only; open‑answer generation possible but not evaluated.
• 10‑question length; longer or adaptive tests were not studied.
• Constant ability assumption (θ) across semester tiers; randomised assignment not done. | | **Implications** | • Demonstrates feasibility of real‑time, high‑quality, course‑specific assessments at scale, potentially alleviating instructor workload.
• Points toward future work: fine‑tuning LLMs on locale‑specific data, generating other modalities (short answer, programming diagnostics), and adaptive testing.
• Suggests that AI‑assisted exam design can produce items that are not only passable but potentially better discriminating than many expert‑crafted items. | Candidate B: **Summary** **Main contributions** 1. Introduces an *iterative refinement* (Self‑Refine‑style) pipeline that uses a large language model both as a **question generator** and as an **automatic judge** to produce short, course‑specific multiple‑choice exams. 2. Provides one of the largest real‑world evaluations of LLM‑generated assessment items: ~1 200 students in 71 college courses received AI‑generated exams, while 20 statistics courses (≈ 500 students) served as a benchmark using expert‑written AP‑Statistics items. 3. Demonstrates that AI‑generated items can achieve psychometric quality (difficulty and discrimination) comparable to, or even superior to, human‑crafted standardized‑test items. **Methodology** *Data & prompting* – Instructors supplied course description, syllabus, and prior homework/exams as plain‑text context. Prompt templates gave the generator five “good” example questions (from a 2012 AP Statistics exam) and, after each iteration, added the most recent “good” and “bad” examples judged by the AI‑judge. *Two‑stage generation* – 1. **Question generation loop** – Repeatedly: - Generate one MCQ. - Have the AI‑judge label it “keep” (good) or “remove” (bad) based on relevance, originality, and appropriateness. - Feed the labeled example back into the next prompt (self‑refinement). - Continue until 20 “good” items are collected. 2. **Exam assembly** – The 20 items are re‑judged for difficulty, correctness, and fit; the 10 hardest approved items become the final 10‑question exam. If >10 items are rejected, another batch of 20 is generated and the process repeats. *Benchmark creation* – For the 20 statistics courses, 24 AP‑Statistics MCQs were filtered (text‑only) and an LLM selected the 10 most concept‑aligned, difficulty‑calibrated items for each class. *Evaluation* – All students (≈ 1 686) completed a common pre‑test plus the semester‑end exam. A hierarchical Bayesian 2‑parameter IRT model (discrimination α, difficulty β) was fit jointly to pre‑test and exam responses, providing: - Item‑level β and α estimates. - Test‑information curves and conditional reliability R(θ). **Key findings** | Metric (averaged over items) | AI‑generated | AP‑Statistics (human) | |------------------------------|--------------|-----------------------| | Difficulty β (mean) | –0.45 (≈ 60 % correct) | +0.35 (≈ 39 % correct) | | Discrimination α (mean) | 1.3 | 1.2 | | Proportion “high/very‑high” discriminating | 36 % | 21 % | | Max test information I_max (exam) | 3.85 → R≈ 0.79 (peak at θ≈ –0.5) | 2.61 → R≈ 0.72 (peak at θ≈ +0.3) | *Interpretation* - **Difficulty**: AI items were on average easier (negative β) than the expert items, reflecting the generator’s anchoring to instructor‑provided materials. - **Discrimination**: AI items showed slightly higher α values; a larger share achieved “high” or “very‑high” discrimination, indicating they separate stronger from weaker students more effectively. - **Test information**: Exams built from AI items provided greater overall information and reliability, especially for students of slightly below‑average ability, while still covering the full ability range. **Conclusion** The study shows that a modestly‑prompted LLM, coupled with an automatic self‑refinement loop, can produce short, course‑specific multiple‑choice exams whose psychometric properties rival those of human‑crafted standardized items. This suggests a viable pathway for scaling high‑quality, customized assessments, reducing instructor workload, and expanding access to tailored testing across diverse subjects.
